chapter_theme: Sayambavai, watching from her mansion, sees the princes ride in and is taken by Tivittan; the Vidyadhara king and Prajapati exchange greetings and she is given to Prajapati, who declares the match the fruit of Tivittan's austerity, after which she laments her love on the terrace.

cast.role: Prajapati, king of Podanam, father of Vijayan and Tivittan
the Vidyadhara king, lord of the hill, Sayambavai's father
Prajapati's younger son, the dark prince Sayambavai loves
Arkakirti, the Vidyadhara king's son, riding with the princes
the Vidyadhara king's daughter, the bride
Sayambavai's friend, who names the princes
the girl's women and mothers who attend her

970.reading: Prajapati greets the Vidyadhara king, who came down from the sky like the lord of the gods and thought him worth the visit, and addresses him as lord of rutting elephants with fire in his eyes.
970.nuance: The speaker is not named in the verse; the address in line 4 and the host's welcome in the next verses fix him as Prajapati. The third line is hard and its sense is held loosely.
970.event: Prajapati welcomes the Vidyadhara king, who has descended from the sky to Podanam.

971.reading: The Vidyadhara king answers, hailing Prajapati as bull of the Ikshvaku kings and lord of Suramai, and says that those who went to the holy waters of nectar went to cleanse, which belongs to the highest of the world.
971.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are obscure, and the compressed image of the nectar-waters is read here only in outline.
971.event: The Vidyadhara king replies to Prajapati's welcome with praise of his house.

972.reading: The Vidyadhara king says that Marusi had come ahead and told him, and that he has come gladly to give his rare daughter to the dark-hued prince, so delay should end.
972.nuance: This is the fulfilment of the astrologer's dream-reading that a Vidyadhara king would come and give a daughter; the king presents it as his own pleasure and not as a fate laid on him.
972.event: The Vidyadhara king says he has come to give his daughter to Tivittan and asks that there be no delay.

973.reading: When the kings have finished talking, the gem-mountain's king sends the princes with Arukkan into the new city, and they ride off on elephants.
973.event: The Vidyadhara king bids the princes and Arkakirti enter the new city, and they ride away on elephants.

974.reading: As the lion-like princes pass, the lord of the silver hill reaches the gem-set palace where his daughter, soft as nectar, waits.
974.nuance: The vimana and the sense of who reaches it are not fully clear in line 4.
974.event: The Vidyadhara king arrives at the mansion where Sayambavai is, while the princes pass.

975.reading: With golden vessels ringing and her girls calling praises about her, bees humming over her garland and hair, she climbs to the seventh storey, a slight woman like a peahen rising to a mountain peak.
975.event: Sayambavai climbs to the seventh storey of the golden mansion among her women.

976.reading: Her friend Amirtha-pirapai opens the jewelled door and, bidding her look at the city, points out the princes riding below.
976.event: The friend opens the door and shows Sayambavai the princes passing near the palace.

977.reading: The princes pass with drums and conches that sound like the sea and shake the earth, and the friend answers the girl, whose mind wonders who they are.
977.event: Sayambavai wonders who the riders are, and the friend answers.

978.reading: The friend names them: the first the sun-named prince with drum-like shoulders, then Prajapati's son, and his dark-cloud younger brother; Sayambavai gives a bright smile.
978.nuance: Which brother is named in each clause turns on the word division of lines 1 and 2, so the order is read tentatively.
978.event: The friend identifies the three princes to Sayambavai, who smiles.

979.reading: The dark-skinned prince with saffron-smeared shoulders draws her eyes, and she cannot call them back and becomes greatly dazed in her heart.
979.nuance: Neither her face nor his is held back by modesty here; the lines present the pull as one-sided, from her eyes to him.
979.event: Sayambavai's eyes turn to Tivittan and she cannot look away.

980.reading: With lotus eyes, long arms, coral mouth and fresh flowers in his hair, the lad shows his charms and takes her eyes captive.
980.event: Tivittan's looks take Sayambavai's eyes captive.

981.reading: The poet argues that there is no restraint once desire rises straight on, and the girl's rare restraint has gone to the fragrant-haired lord.
981.nuance: The verse rests on a play of 'siRai' (a captive, a bank) and 'niRai' (restraint, fullness), as a river's flood overruns its banks; the argument is the poet's and is not put in her mouth.

claims.claim: restraint cannot hold when desire rises unopposed

982.reading: As the lad turns his moon-bright face and sniffs a flower, his gaze draws her, and modesty holds her back while she melts between the two.
982.event: Tivittan looks at Sayambavai and smells a flower while her modesty holds her back.

983.reading: Hearing her father call her this way, the dark-eyed girl, with the prince in her heart, goes off with modesty as the curtain that hides him.
983.nuance: The first line is read as the father calling her; the lines have a repaired pulli in line 2.
983.event: Sayambavai goes to her father at his call, hiding her feeling behind modesty.

984.reading: Surrounded by girls with bamboo shoulders, she goes and bows at the feet of her father, rich as a gem-set rod from a red hill.
984.event: Sayambavai bows at her father's feet.

985.reading: The father seats her on his right, sets her garland, hair and ear-ring right with his hand and bids her bow at her uncle's feet, then lays her at the feet of the lord of the lotus-ponded land.
985.nuance: 'Maaman' here is Prajapati, to whom she is given as bride for his son; the kinship term is the speech's own.
985.event: The Vidyadhara king sets Sayambavai right and places her at Prajapati's feet.

986.reading: Prajapati seats the girl on his right thigh, looks at her great beauty, and says the lad who wins this goddess must have great earlier austerity and surely will rule the wheel.
986.nuance: This answers the earlier reading that Tivittan will protect the whole joined world, and ties the girl's coming to his merit.
986.event: Prajapati takes Sayambavai on his thigh and declares Tivittan will rule the wheel.

claims.claim: great earlier austerity wins the bride and with her sovereignty

987.reading: Prajapati asks whether the Maker gathered every beauty fit for jewelled women and set it in her, or whether every great woman's form entered her, so that the world could see.
987.nuance: The idea of the Maker is a figure of praise and no claim of a creator god in a Jain epic; no school is claimed.

988.reading: Prajapati says he must have rare austerity, or else would the words that he is the father of such a woman and the divine wealth and bond come to him?
988.nuance: The speaker is not named; the 'father' in line 2 may be either king, so the reading is held loosely.

claims.claim: a worthy bride, wealth and kin come only to one of rare austerity

989.reading: After the kings have talked, the girl, her women and mothers attending her, is sent to the golden city and reaches the white-moonlit terrace of the shining palace.
989.event: Sayambavai is sent on to the golden city and climbs to the palace terrace.

990.reading: The girl, burning inwardly, says that if she forgot the garlanded man, fate would drive her back to remember him, and asks whether the world knows this.
990.nuance: The stanza was printed in eight half-lines and has been joined.
990.event: Sayambavai laments on the terrace that she cannot forget Tivittan.

claims.claim: fate presses the mind to remember the beloved

991.reading: The poet, or the girl, says that looking at lovers whom love has made dear as if they were strangers doubles the pain, since the love-god's arrow makes a target of such looks, so love's sickness has no rare medicine.

992.reading: Groves, sandy shore, hills and pools give no shelter to those who enter, and mind, eye and restraint no longer stay their own, so who can be a refuge for the lovesick?

claims.claim: those with desire in their mind have no refuge in places or in themselves

links.note: Soolamani 107 has the astrologer read a dream as a Vidyadhara king coming to praise the lord and give a daughter; here he arrives at Podanam and says he has come gladly to give her.
links.teaches: The reading of the dream is kept in the king's own gladness, so the prophecy is borne out as willing consent and not only as outcome.

links.note: Soolamani 109 has the court confirm that Tivittan will guard the whole world under one umbrella; here Prajapati, holding the bride, says that his earlier austerity is the reason and that the wheel is certain.
links.teaches: The prophecy gets a cause in Tivittan's earlier austerity, which the court's earlier confirmation lacked.

links.note: Kural 1251 has the axe of desire break the door of restraint bolted with shame; Soolamani 981 has restraint vanish because desire runs straight on, and puts it in the poet's voice about the girl.
links.teaches: The Kural gives restraint a lock that desire can break, while the Jain epic says the restraint was not broken but given to the one she loves.

gains.a: The verse lacks a picture of how restraint fails; the couplet gives the door, the bolt and the axe.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where the woman's restraint is not lost to chance but handed to a particular lover, and the poet argues it a worthy gift.

links.note: Kural 1094 has the man see that when he looks she looks at the ground, and when he does not she smiles; in 982 the lad looks boldly while her modesty holds her back and she melts.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the lover's inference from the lowered eye, and the epic shows the same shyness from within, as a pull she cannot hide.

gains.a: The verse lacks the timing of looking and looking away that tells the watcher she is moved.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the girl's inner melting and the power of her modesty over her, which the epic shows.

links.note: Kural 1125 has the man say he would recall her only if he forgot, but he does not know how to forget; 990 has the girl say that if she tried to forget, fate itself would drive her back to remember.
links.teaches: Both deny forgetting, but the Soolamani lays the compulsion on fate, which the Kural leaves to the lover's nature.

gains.a: The verse lacks the compact logic that remembering needs a prior forgetting.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a cause for the failure to forget; the verse supplies fate, and the girl's inward cry that the world does not know it.

links.note: Kural 1102 says the cure for a disease is usually other than its cause but this woman is herself the cure for the sickness she brings; Soolamani 991 says love's sickness has no cure and that looking coolly at loved ones only doubles the wound.
links.teaches: The Kural finds the remedy in union with the beloved, and the epic denies any remedy before the union.

gains.a: The verse lacks the possibility of a cure in the beloved, which the couplet names.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the stage before union, where the girl sees no cure and fear doubles the pain.

links.note: Naladiyar 47 has the fool call a body of nine seeping openings 'broad-shouldered one, bangle-wearer' because skin dazzles his eyes; Soolamani 987 has Prajapati marvel that the Maker gathered all beauty into one girl.
links.teaches: The same dazzled look at a woman is a fool's error in the Naladiyar and a bride's honour in the epic, so the epic's praise stands on a view of the body the Jain text refuses.

gains.a: The verse lacks the view of the body as flesh that the epic's praise leaves out.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a case where the praise of a woman's beauty is made by a worldly king and so shows what it attacks.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 204 tells the heart to turn away from smiling women as the etti fruit is poison under a good look; Soolamani 980 shows a man's looks seize a girl's eyes and holds the pull as natural.
links.teaches: The epic tells love as a force that wins the heart, and Tirumular gives the warning that such pull is the poison.

gains.a: The verse lacks any warning that the seizing of the eyes may harm.
gains.b: The poem lacks a case that shows the pull working, from the woman's side.

links.note: Soolamani 155 has her modesty make a flower-vine droop in shame; here modesty is the curtain she draws round the prince she carries in her heart.
links.teaches: Modesty shifts from an ornament of her beauty into the screen that hides her love.

source_issues: Verses 981 and 983 had a pulli after a vowel sign removed; verse 990 is printed as eight half-lines and was joined into four.
